title: Recommender Systems
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Recommender Systems ##### The recommender that only recommended what was already selling A grocery delivery app in Bengaluru launched a "recommended for you" carousel. Offline evaluation looked strong — RMSE on held-out ratings of 0.84, comfortably better than the baseline. Three months in, the carousel's contribution to revenue was 1.2%, and the catalogue had visibly narrowed. Items outside the top 400 SKUs were almost never shown, new products took months to gain any traction, and long-tail suppliers were complaining. Two things had gone wrong, and both are structural rather than accidental. They had optimised **rating prediction** when the product needed **ranking**. RMSE rewards getting 3.2 versus 3.4 right on items nobody will see; nobody cares about the model's accuracy on position 800. What matters is whether the top five are good. And the model had no mechanism for **cold start**. A new item has no interaction history, so collaborative filtering assigns it nothing, so it is never shown, so it never accumulates history. The feedback loop is self-reinforcing. Rebuilding around ranking metrics with a content-based cold-start path took the carousel to 8.4% of revenue and restored catalogue coverage. Recommenders are where offline metrics and business value diverge most sharply. Today is about closing that gap. ##### Content-based versus collaborative Two fundamentally different sources of signal. **Content-based filtering** recommends items similar to what a user liked, using item *attributes*. If you bought organic turmeric, here are other organic spices. **Collaborative filtering** recommends what similar *users* liked, using the interaction matrix alone. Users who bought what you bought also bought this. | | Content-based | Collaborative | |---|---|---| | Uses | Item features | Interaction patterns | | New item (cold start) | **Works immediately** | Fails completely | | New user | Needs one interaction | Fails until several | | Serendipity | Low — stays in a niche | High — crosses categories | | Explainability | Easy: "similar to X" | Harder | | Data requirement | Good item metadata | Dense interaction history | | Popularity bias | Low | **High** | ```python import numpy as np, pandas as pd from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity # Content-based: item similarity from text and attributes items["profile"] = (items["category"] + " " + items["brand"] + " " + items["tags"].fillna("") + " " + items["description"].fillna("")) tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(max_features=8_000, ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=3, stop_words="english") item_vectors = tfidf.fit_transform(items["profile"]) item_sim = cosine_similarity(item_vectors, dense_output=False) def content_recommend(item_id: int, k: int = 10) -> pd.DataFrame: idx = item_index[item_id] scores = np.asarray(item_sim[idx].todense()).ravel() scores[idx] = -1 # exclude the item itself top = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:k] return items.iloc[top].assign(similarity=scores[top]) def user_profile_recommend(user_id: int, k: int = 10): """Build a user vector as the weighted average of items they liked.""" liked = interactions[(interactions.user_id == user_id) & (interactions.rating >= 4)] if liked.empty: return popularity_baseline(k) idxs = [item_index[i] for i in liked.item_id] weights = liked.rating.to_numpy().reshape(-1, 1) profile = (item_vectors[idxs].multiply(weights)).sum(axis=0) / weights.sum() scores = cosine_similarity(np.asarray(profile), item_vectors).ravel() scores[idxs] = -1 # exclude already-seen return items.iloc[np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:k]] ``` **Collaborative filtering** in its simplest form is neighbourhood-based: ```python from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix # User-item matrix, sparse because almost every cell is empty R = csr_matrix((interactions.rating, (interactions.user_idx, interactions.item_idx)), shape=(n_users, n_items)) print(f"sparsity: {1 - R.nnz / (n_users * n_items):.4%}") # Item-item CF: usually better than user-user (items are more stable than tastes) item_similarity = cosine_similarity(R.T, dense_output=False) def item_cf_recommend(user_idx: int, k: int = 10): user_row = R[user_idx].toarray().ravel() scores = item_similarity.dot(user_row) scores[user_row > 0] = -np.inf # exclude seen items return np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:k] ``` Real interaction matrices are typically 99.5% to 99.99% empty, which is why sparse representations are mandatory rather than an optimisation. **Item-item collaborative filtering usually outperforms user-user**, for a practical reason: item similarity is more stable over time than user taste, so it can be precomputed and cached. Amazon's classic recommendation system was built on exactly this. ##### Matrix factorization The core idea: approximate the sparse interaction matrix `R` as the product of two dense low-rank matrices. ``` R (n_users × n_items) ≈ P (n_users × k) · Qᵀ (k × n_items) r̂ᵤᵢ = pᵤ · qᵢ + bᵤ + bᵢ + μ ``` Each user and item is represented by a `k`-dimensional **latent factor** vector. Those factors are learned, not designed — and they often turn out to correspond to interpretable dimensions like price sensitivity, spiciness preference, or brand loyalty. The bias terms matter more than beginners expect. `μ` is the global mean, `bᵤ` captures that some users rate everything highly, and `bᵢ` captures that some items are simply better. Koren et al. found that biases alone explain a large fraction of the variance, before any personalisation. ```python from surprise import SVD, Dataset, Reader, accuracy from surprise.model_selection import cross_validate, train_test_split reader = Reader(rating_scale=(1, 5)) data = Dataset.load_from_df(interactions[["user_id", "item_id", "rating"]], reader) trainset, testset = train_test_split(data, test_size=0.2, random_state=42) svd = SVD(n_factors=100, n_epochs=30, lr_all=0.005, reg_all=0.05, biased=True, random_state=42) svd.fit(trainset) preds = svd.test(testset) print(f"RMSE {accuracy.rmse(preds, verbose=False):.4f}") ``` **For implicit feedback** — clicks, views, purchases, watch time — the problem changes fundamentally. There are no negative ratings; an absence of interaction means "not seen" or "not interested" and you cannot tell which. Hu, Koren and Volinsky's **ALS for implicit feedback** handles this by treating all unobserved entries as weak negatives, weighted by a confidence derived from interaction strength: ```python import implicit from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix # Confidence weighting: c = 1 + alpha * interaction_count alpha = 40 C = csr_matrix((1 + alpha * interactions.n_purchases, (interactions.user_idx, interactions.item_idx)), shape=(n_users, n_items)) model = implicit.als.AlternatingLeastSquares( factors=128, regularization=0.05, iterations=25, use_gpu=False, calculate_training_loss=True, random_state=42, ) model.fit(C) item_ids, scores = model.recommend(user_idx, C[user_idx], N=10, filter_already_liked_items=True) # Similar items — useful for a "customers also viewed" module similar, sim_scores = model.similar_items(item_idx, N=10) ``` **ALS is the workhorse for implicit feedback at scale.** It alternates between solving for user factors with item factors fixed and vice versa, each step being a closed-form least-squares solve, which parallelises trivially. **BPR** (Bayesian Personalised Ranking) is the alternative: instead of predicting values, it directly optimises the *ordering* — for each user, a purchased item should rank above a non-purchased one. ```python bpr = implicit.bpr.BayesianPersonalizedRanking(factors=128, learning_rate=0.01, regularization=0.01, iterations=100, random_state=42) bpr.fit(C) ``` **BPR optimises ranking directly, which is what the Bengaluru team needed.** If your product shows a top-k list, a pairwise ranking objective aligns better with the goal than a pointwise rating objective. ##### Implicit feedback and cold start Implicit feedback dominates real systems — explicit ratings are rare, biased toward extremes, and expensive to collect. Converting raw signals into a confidence matrix requires judgement: ```python def build_confidence(events: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame: """Weight different interaction types by how much intent they signal.""" weights = {"view": 1.0, "add_to_cart": 4.0, "purchase": 10.0, "return": -5.0} events["weight"] = events["event_type"].map(weights) # Time decay — recent behaviour matters more days_ago = (events["ts"].max() - events["ts"]).dt.days events["weight"] *= np.exp(-days_ago / 60) # 60-day half-life-ish conf = (events.groupby(["user_idx", "item_idx"])["weight"].sum() .clip(lower=0).reset_index()) return conf[conf.weight > 0] ``` Two design points. **Negative signals** (returns, quick bounces, explicit dismissals) carry real information and are usually discarded. And **time decay** matters because a purchase from two years ago says less about current preference than one from last week. **Cold start** comes in three flavours, each needing a different answer: ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Cold start] --> B{What is new?} B -->|New item, no interactions| C[Content-based from metadata] C --> D[Also: exploration slots in the ranking] B -->|New user, no history| E[Popularity + demographic segment] E --> F[Onboarding: ask for 3-5 preferences] B -->|New system, no data| G[Content-based + business rules] G --> H[Log everything from day one] ``` ```python def recommend_with_cold_start(user_id, k=10, exploration_slots=2): """Hybrid recommender that degrades gracefully and reserves exploration.""" n_interactions = interaction_counts.get(user_id, 0) if n_interactions == 0: base = popularity_by_segment(user_segment(user_id), k=k - exploration_slots) elif n_interactions < 5: # Blend: content-based dominates until CF has enough signal w_cf = n_interactions / 5 base = blend(content_recommend_for_user(user_id, k * 2), cf_recommend(user_id, k * 2), weights=(1 - w_cf, w_cf), k=k - exploration_slots) else: base = cf_recommend(user_id, k - exploration_slots) # ALWAYS reserve slots for cold items — this breaks the feedback loop cold = sample_cold_items(user_id, n=exploration_slots) return interleave(base, cold) ``` **The exploration slots are the part the Bengaluru team was missing.** Reserving two of ten positions for items with little history costs a small amount of immediate relevance and prevents the catalogue collapse. Without deliberate exploration, a recommender converges on whatever was already popular and stays there. For new items specifically, **content-to-latent mapping** bridges the gap: ```python from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge # Learn to predict an item's latent factors from its metadata warm_items = [i for i in items.index if interaction_counts_item[i] >= 20] mapper = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit( item_features[warm_items], # metadata: category, brand, price, text model.item_factors[warm_items], # learned CF factors ) # For a new item, predict its factors and place it in the same latent space new_item_factors = mapper.predict(item_features[[new_item_idx]]) ``` That approach lets a new item participate in collaborative recommendations from day one, using its metadata to estimate where it sits in the learned latent space. ##### Ranking metrics The Bengaluru failure. RMSE measures rating accuracy; users experience a **ranked list**. ```python def precision_at_k(recommended: list, relevant: set, k: int) -> float: """Of the top k shown, what fraction were relevant?""" top_k = recommended[:k] return len(set(top_k) & relevant) / k if k else 0.0 def recall_at_k(recommended: list, relevant: set, k: int) -> float: """Of all relevant items, what fraction appeared in the top k?""" if not relevant: return 0.0 return len(set(recommended[:k]) & relevant) / len(relevant) def average_precision_at_k(recommended: list, relevant: set, k: int) -> float: """Rewards putting relevant items EARLY in the list.""" if not relevant: return 0.0 hits, score = 0, 0.0 for i, item in enumerate(recommended[:k], start=1): if item in relevant: hits += 1 score += hits / i return score / min(len(relevant), k) def ndcg_at_k(recommended: list, relevance: dict, k: int) -> float: """Normalised discounted cumulative gain — handles graded relevance.""" dcg = sum(relevance.get(item, 0) / np.log2(i + 1) for i, item in enumerate(recommended[:k], start=1)) ideal = sorted(relevance.values(), reverse=True)[:k] idcg = sum(rel / np.log2(i + 1) for i, rel in enumerate(ideal, start=1)) return dcg / idcg if idcg > 0 else 0.0 ``` | Metric | Answers | Sensitive to position? | |---|---|---| | Precision@k | How much of what we showed was good? | No | | Recall@k | How much of the good stuff did we show? | No | | MAP@k | Did we put the good items early? | **Yes** | | NDCG@k | Same, with graded relevance | **Yes** | | MRR | How high was the first relevant item? | Yes | | Hit rate@k | Did we get at least one right? | No | **NDCG is the standard for ranking** because the logarithmic discount matches how attention actually decays down a list — position 1 matters far more than position 8. And unlike MAP, it handles graded relevance, so a five-star item ranking above a three-star one is rewarded. Beyond accuracy, three metrics that would have caught the catalogue collapse: ```python def coverage(all_recommendations: list[list], n_items: int) -> float: """What fraction of the catalogue ever gets recommended?""" return len({i for recs in all_recommendations for i in recs}) / n_items def novelty(all_recommendations: list[list], popularity: dict) -> float: """Mean self-information — higher means less popular items.""" return np.mean([-np.log2(popularity.get(i, 1e-9)) for recs in all_recommendations for i in recs]) def intra_list_diversity(recommendations: list, sim_matrix) -> float: """1 - mean pairwise similarity within a single list.""" idxs = [item_index[i] for i in recommendations] sims = [sim_matrix[a, b] for a in idxs for b in idxs if a < b] return 1 - np.mean(sims) if sims else 0.0 def gini_coefficient(recommendation_counts: np.ndarray) -> float: """0 = perfectly even exposure, 1 = all recommendations go to one item.""" x = np.sort(recommendation_counts) n = len(x) return (2 * np.sum((np.arange(1, n + 1)) * x) / (n * np.sum(x))) - (n + 1) / n ``` **Coverage and Gini are the diagnostic pair.** A recommender with excellent NDCG and 4% coverage is concentrating all exposure on a handful of items, which is exactly what happened in Bengaluru. Track them alongside accuracy, always. **Evaluation protocol matters as much as the metric.** Random splitting of interactions leaks future behaviour into training: ```python def leave_last_n_out(interactions: pd.DataFrame, n: int = 1): """Per user, hold out their n most recent interactions.""" interactions = interactions.sort_values(["user_id", "ts"]) test = interactions.groupby("user_id").tail(n) train = interactions.drop(test.index) return train, test def temporal_split(interactions: pd.DataFrame, cutoff: str): """Global time cutoff — the most realistic protocol.""" return (interactions[interactions.ts < cutoff], interactions[interactions.ts >= cutoff]) ``` **Use a global temporal split** for anything you will deploy. Leave-one-out is common in papers and optimistic, because it lets the model train on a user's future behaviour to predict their past. And always compare against a **popularity baseline**: ```python def popularity_baseline(k=10): return interactions.item_id.value_counts().head(k).index.tolist() ``` Popularity is a genuinely strong baseline. A personalised recommender that does not beat it on NDCG is not adding value, and this comparison is skipped surprisingly often. ##### Hybrid and modern approaches Production systems combine signals, and the standard architecture is two-stage. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Full catalogue
100k+ items] --> B[CANDIDATE GENERATION] B --> B1[Collaborative filtering: 200] B --> B2[Content similarity: 100] B --> B3[Popular in segment: 50] B --> B4[Recently viewed / cart: 30] B --> B5[Exploration: cold items 20] B1 --> C[~400 candidates, deduplicated] B2 --> C B3 --> C B4 --> C B5 --> C C --> D[RANKING: learning-to-rank model
with rich features] D --> E[Business rules: stock, margin,
diversity, blocklist] E --> F[Final top 10] ``` **Candidate generation** is cheap and recall-oriented — several complementary sources each contributing a few hundred items. **Ranking** is expensive and precision-oriented, applying a full-featured model to only those candidates. The ranking stage is a supervised learning problem with all the features you have: ```python import lightgbm as lgb def build_ranking_features(user_id, candidate_ids): return pd.DataFrame({ "cf_score": [cf_scores.get((user_id, i), 0) for i in candidate_ids], "content_sim": [content_scores.get((user_id, i), 0) for i in candidate_ids], "item_popularity": [popularity[i] for i in candidate_ids], "item_ctr_30d": [item_ctr[i] for i in candidate_ids], "price_vs_user_avg": [prices[i] / user_avg_price[user_id] for i in candidate_ids], "category_affinity": [user_cat_affinity.get((user_id, cat[i]), 0) for i in candidate_ids], "days_since_launch": [item_age[i] for i in candidate_ids], "in_stock": [stock[i] > 0 for i in candidate_ids], }) # LambdaRank optimises NDCG directly ranker = lgb.LGBMRanker( objective="lambdarank", metric="ndcg", ndcg_eval_at=[5, 10], n_estimators=600, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42, verbose=-1, ) ranker.fit(X_train, y_train, group=group_sizes_train, eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)], eval_group=[group_sizes_val], callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100, verbose=False)]) ``` `LGBMRanker` with `objective="lambdarank"` optimises NDCG directly rather than a pointwise loss — the same insight as BPR, applied to a feature-rich model. Modern architectures worth knowing by name: **two-tower neural networks** (separate user and item encoders producing embeddings compared by dot product, which allows precomputing item vectors and using ANN search at serving time), **sequential models** (SASRec, BERT4Rec, treating a user's interaction history as a sequence), and **graph neural networks** (LightGCN, propagating signal over the user-item bipartite graph). The honest assessment: **matrix factorisation plus a good ranking model with strong features beats most neural architectures on most business problems**, and it is dramatically easier to operate. Reach for the sophisticated approaches when you have tens of millions of interactions and a dedicated team. ##### Common mistakes - Optimising RMSE when the product shows a ranked list. - No popularity baseline, so the value of personalisation is unmeasured. - Random interaction splits, leaking future behaviour into training. - No coverage or Gini tracking, so catalogue collapse goes unnoticed. - No exploration slots, creating a self-reinforcing popularity loop. - Treating unobserved implicit interactions as confirmed negatives. - No cold-start path, so new items are structurally invisible. - Recommending items the user already owns or that are out of stock. - Dense matrices on a 99.9% sparse problem, exhausting memory. - Deploying without an A/B test, since offline ranking gains often do not transfer. ##### Hands-on Build a collaborative-filtering recommender with matrix factorisation on a ratings dataset and a content-based recommender on the same data. Evaluate both with Precision@k, NDCG@k and MAP@k under a temporal split, and compare against a popularity baseline. Then compute coverage and Gini for each — the gap between the accuracy ranking and the coverage ranking is the lesson, because the model that looks best on NDCG is frequently the one concentrating exposure on the head of the catalogue. For the mini-project, build a hybrid recommender combining collaborative and content-based signals with an explicit cold-start path for new items and new users, plus reserved exploration slots. Evaluate with ranking metrics against a popularity baseline under a global temporal split, and report coverage, novelty and intra-list diversity alongside accuracy. Include a two-stage architecture with candidate generation and a LambdaRank ranker, and a section analysing what fraction of the catalogue your system would ever show — the Bengaluru number was 4%, and finding your own is the point. For the assignment, explain the cold-start problem and describe two concrete strategies to mitigate it. Cover all three flavours (new item, new user, new system), and be specific about the feedback-loop mechanism that makes cold start self-reinforcing rather than merely inconvenient. ##### Key takeaways - Optimise ranking, not rating prediction — NDCG and MAP reward getting the top of the list right, which is what users experience. - Content-based handles cold start; collaborative finds serendipitous patterns; production systems need both. - For implicit feedback, use confidence-weighted ALS or a pairwise objective like BPR rather than treating absence as a negative. - Track coverage, novelty and Gini alongside accuracy, and reserve exploration slots to break the popularity feedback loop. - Split temporally, always compare against popularity, and validate offline gains with an online A/B test.
practical_task_reference: Build a collaborative-filtering recommender with matrix factorization on a ratings dataset (e.g., MovieLens) and a content-based recommender, then evaluate both with Precision@k and NDCG.
mini_project_reference: Build a hybrid recommender that combines collaborative and content-based signals, handles cold-start for new items, and is evaluated with ranking metrics against a popularity baseline.
assignment_reference: Explain the cold-start problem and describe two concrete strategies to mitigate it.
